content:
<<Nightwatch of a Hundred>>

It began as one of those sporting scenes that invite the wrong kind of sympathy. People projected their own nerves onto him, imagining a young batter marooned on a precarious score, alone with the weight of tomorrow. He had surged late on the first evening, riding a partnership that resuscitated a listing innings, and then he was left to sleep on the promise. A first hundred hung in the air like a storm that might never break.

The doom-mongers pictured tosses and turns, a mind gnawed by possibility, hands that might feel too tight around the handle come morning. But when he walked out beneath the pale sky, there was no wobble in his stride. The first ball whispered past his hips and he feathered it fine for four; the next he carved through cover, smooth as a practiced signature. If the night had tried to creep under his skin, daylight had burned it away.

Even luck toyed with him and blinked first. An appeal that looked ominous unraveled on review, the imagined red of leg stump dissolving into safety, and a skidding inside edge missed the woodwork by a coat of paint. All the while the fielders frayed, lines loosened, and the outfield flashed back every clean strike like a mirror to his intent. He played with tempo and touch, daring yet balanced, the crowd learning his name syllable by syllable with each boundary.

chain of moments, that’s what a hundred truly is: not a stat, but a rosary of decisions, threaded by breath and belief. He reached it with a drive that hummed past mid-off, the ball fizzing into applause and relief. Then he followed it with a pull that sounded like an oath—crisp, declarative, a sentence answered with a full stop. The dressing room balcony scattered into smiles and fist pumps; the stadium felt closer, conspiratorial.

There are cricketers who survive long enough to be seen, and cricketers who, in an instant, demand to be watched. He joined the latter. The fear others gifted him had never been unwrapped; the night’s questions found their answers in morning’s strokes. And when he finally tucked his bat beneath his arm, the pitch seemed a little shorter, the crowd a little fuller, and the day, at last, entirely his.
